svg.title: Exchanges the harness performs against an independently developed HL7 Da Vinci payer
svg.desc: Three exchanges across a process boundary between the Cloud Health Office interoperability harness on the left and the pinned HL7 Da Vinci burden-reduction payer reference implementation on the right. First, PAS: Cloud Health Office posts a synthetic prior-authorization bundle to the payer's Claim dollar-submit and parses the returned PAS response with the same FHIR parser its own service uses. Second, CRD: Cloud Health Office fetches the payer's CDS Hooks discovery document, resolves the order-sign service by hook rather than by list position, and invokes it with three synthetic draft orders carrying different billing codes; the payer's own rules return three genuinely different coverage determinations, and one of them names a DTR questionnaire canonical. Third, DTR: Cloud Health Office takes that canonical — the one the payer chose — and requests exactly it from the payer's questionnaire-package operation, then checks that every dependency the returned questionnaire declares resolves inside the package. A note records that a CRD determination can arrive in the system action rather than in cards, and that the payer's rules are never reimplemented inside Cloud Health Office.
svg.text: payer server · software CHO does not own
A REAL PROCESS BOUNDARY — NOTHING MOCKED OR REPLAYED
POST Claim/$submit — a synthetic prior-authorization bundle
PAS response bundle, parsed and validated with the same FHIR parser CHO's own service runs
GET /cds-services, then POST the order-sign service resolved from discovery by hook
three billing codes, three different determinations from the payer's own rules — one names a questionnaire canonical
POST Questionnaire/$questionnaire-package — for exactly the canonical the payer just named
the package bundle, checked so every dependency the questionnaire declares resolves inside it
the payer chooses the questionnaire; CHO follows it
A CRD determination can arrive in the system action rather than in cards. A client that inspected only cards would conclude nothing happened.
The payer's rules are never reimplemented inside Cloud Health Office. Protocol interoperability is not payer rule parity.
